paras: The lynching of Crane Green was the hanging of a Black mill worker by a mob near Warren, Arkansas, on the night of Sunday, July 19, 1903. Accused of assaulting a 13-year-old white girl, Green was taken from officers who were bringing him to jail and hanged from a tree beside the Kingsland road. The lynchers were not identified, and the Associated Press carried the event to papers across the country in a single sentence datelined Pine Bluff.

Green worked at Childs' mill, about nine miles northwest of Warren, according to a Warren special to the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic. On Saturday, July 18, he was accused of assaulting a girl of 13 named Blake, the daughter of a white employee at the mill. A Warren dispatch printed in the Newport Independent gave a different version, naming him John Green and the girl as the 14-year-old daughter of W. E. Baker, and saying she was alone because the mill had shut down for the day.

After Green fled, officers telephoned to every point in the county and people throughout it watched for him. He was found at Lanark on Sunday, where officers arrested him and started back toward the jail at Warren. The Newport account instead said that pursuing parties of men captured him near Lanark that morning.

On the way back the officers were met by a mob, which took Green from them and hanged him. According to the Graphic's correspondent, the lynchers 'did their work quietly', waiting on the Kingsland road for the officers, hanging Green and dispersing once they were sure he was dead. Nothing was known in Warren until Monday morning, when a farmer came into town and reported a body hanging from a roadside tree about five miles from Kingsland.
The St. Louis Republic reported that the identity of the lynchers was not known. No report of an inquest, arrests or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic ran the story on its front page the next day under the headline 'Lynching Near Warren' with the deck 'Negro Rape Fiend Suffers the Usual Penalty For His Crime', calling the hanging a 'lynching bee'. Other specials, in the St. Louis Republic and the Memphis Commercial-Appeal (reprinted in the Bryan Morning Eagle as 'Strung Him Up'), treated the assault as established and reported the hanging without comment. The Republic's headline stressed that the mob 'Made No Demonstration', and its account was reprinted in the Butler Weekly Times.

Most papers saw only the Associated Press sentence, which ran on July 21 and 22 from Birmingham and New York to Raleigh and Butte, under heads such as 'Negro Lynched' and 'Lynched for an Attack on a Girl'. Weekly news digests reduced it further to 'Negro lynched at Pine Bluff, Ark' or a line saying Green 'was hanged by a mob at Pine Bluff', placing the event at the wire dateline rather than near Warren.

The Worcester Spy took up the brevity of the coverage itself, remarking that 'only a few words about it were telegraphed' and warning that lynchings might soon go unreported, 'so commonplace will they become'.

The reports differ on the victim's first name, with one dispatch calling him John Green, and on the girl's family name and age. They also differ on the night of the lynching: the Warren reports written on July 20 place it on Sunday night, while later wire versions said 'late last night' under a July 21 dateline or 'Monday night', and the Worcester Spy said Tuesday. Placement varies from five miles north of Warren to five miles from Kingsland, which the Commercial-Appeal special put in Cleveland County, and to six miles from Warren near the mill.

reader.title: Lynching of Crane Green
bases: Every account says a mob took Crane Green from officers bringing him to jail and hanged him on an accusation of assault (A1, A2, A4, A12).

Green was hanged by a 'mob' of unidentified men who took him from officers before any trial, as punishment for an alleged assault on a white girl (A2, A4, A5, A12); 'mob' and 'lynchers' in the plural are read as three or more though no number is given.

A Warren special to the Pine Bluff Graphic (A1, A2), a St. Louis Republic special (A4), a Warren dispatch in the Newport Independent (A5), the Memphis Commercial-Appeal special (A12) and the AP (A6) independently report the seizure and hanging.

accounts.label: Warren correspondent (Pine Bluff Graphic)
accounts.gist: Officers arrested Green at Lanark Sunday afternoon and started for the Warren jail; lynchers waited on the Kingsland road, took him, hanged him and quietly dispersed, and the body was reported by a farmer next morning.

accounts.label: Warren dispatch (Newport Independent)
accounts.gist: 'John Green' assaulted W. E. Baker's 14-year-old daughter while the mill was shut down; pursuing parties captured him near Lanark Sunday morning, and a mob hanged him that night about six miles from Warren.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff specials (St. Louis Republic, Commercial-Appeal)
accounts.gist: Green was lynched 'quietly' about five miles from Kingsland after officers who went for him were met by a mob on the way back; the lynchers were not identified.

accounts.label: Associated Press
accounts.gist: One-sentence brief: for an assault on a 13-year-old white girl, Green was taken from officers carrying him to jail and lynched; the night given varies by version.

framing.detail: The Pine Bluff Graphic headlined 'Negro Rape Fiend Suffers the Usual Penalty For His Crime', called the lynching a 'lynching bee' and stated the assault as fact.
The St. Louis Republic ('Lynched Negro in the Night. Mob at Kingsland, Ark., Made No Demonstration') and the Newport Independent reported the accusation as fact and the hanging without comment.
The AP sent a single sentence ('For an assault upon a 13-year-old white girl...') that ran in papers across the country under heads such as 'Negro Lynched' and 'Lynched for an Attack on a Girl'.
The Worcester Spy said only a few words were telegraphed and warned that lynchings might soon go unmentioned 'so commonplace will they become'.
